newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank shares gain as 1996 results impress.
newsitem.headline: German bank shares gain as 1996 results impress.

text.p: German bank shares scored healthy gains on Tuesday after two of the Big Five banks announced results that reflected last year's boom in financial markets and exceeded forecasts.

Deutsche Bank AG stock advanced to its highest level in three years after the market leader reported a 37 percent leap in operating profit to 5.8 billion marks ($3.4 billion) -- as much as one billion marks above average forecasts.
Bavarian mortgage bank Bayerische Vereinsbank AG announced an 18 percent rise in operating profit for last year and a firmly bullish outlook for 1997.
The DAX-100's banking index, which tracks Germany's top financial shares, rose nearly two percent to 1,407.91 after the news, outpacing the blue-chip DAX, which rose 1.4 percent.

Deutsche ended the day up 2.3 percent at 88.35 marks. Commerzbank, which already announced a 22 percent rise in net income, advanced 2.5 percent to 43.70. Vereinsbank, whose results were broadly as expected, was steady at 63.90 marks.

German banks had been widely tipped to report strong figures for 1996 but Deutsche had been expected to lag bahind after a series of blows including fund mismanagement problems at London-based Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).

On an after-tax basis, Deutsche's profits were more or less stagnant at 2.2 billion marks, trailing Commerzbank AG's 22 percent rise in net income and Bayerische Vereinsbank AG's preliminary estimated increase of 30 percent.
Analysts said that without more information from Deutsche, it was hard to explain the sharp divergence between stagnant net earnings and buoyant operating profit.

"A lot remains unclear. It looks as if Morgan Grenfell compensation payments may be responsible for the difference," said Markus Strigl, banking analyst at Trinkaus & Burkhardt in Duesseldorf, who recommends buying Deutsche shares.

The most damaging and expensive of a series of mishaps to hit Deutsche last year, the fund mismanagement problems at MGAM, left Deutsche with an estimated 200 million pound compensation bill. It already provided a net injection of 180 million pounds.
But the bank's strong operating performance nonetheless impressed analysts.

"We will certainly have to alter our (Deutsche) earnings estimates for 1997 and 1998 and in part dramatically," said Georg Kanders, group leader of financial research at WestLB Research, which has Deutsche as a "strong buy".
Vereinsbank's operating profit of 1.6 billion marks proved less surprising, although some analysts had expected higher risk provisions, which were unchanged at 700 million marks.

Vereinsbank's growth came on the back of a seven percent rise in net interest income to 4.8 billion marks and a 14 percent increase to 1.2 billion in net commission income, accompanied by stagnation on risk provisions and moderate administrative expenses.
Strigl said he was keeping a "hold" recommendation on Vereinsbank, whose shares have already risen more than a third since mid-1996 on merger talk.
"The shares are too expensive from a fundamental point of view," Strigl commented.
Vereinsbank chief executive Albrecht Schmidt took the opportunity on Tuesday to stress that the bank aimed to stay independent.
This has become a hot issue since Deutsche Bank last year reported a 5.2 percent stake in the bank, starting a wave of takeover rumours.

Deutsche Bank will elaborate on its results at a news conference on March 26. Germany's last two top banks, Dresdner Bank and Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG, will release earnings data later this week. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
